title: Instructions and context in a prompt

steps.say: This video explains how an application builds the prompt for a language model from instructions, context, and a question.
A language model writes its answer from two sources. The first is the text in its prompt.
The second is its training. Training compresses a large body of text into the parameters of the model, which keep patterns of that text and hold no records.
In this example, a user asks how internet access and economic development have evolved in Rwanda and Kenya.
The prompt holds only the question, so the model answers from its training. The figures arrive as rounded ranges, and none of them carries a citation.
Six figures from that answer are set here beside the official values in World Development Indicators.
Four of the six are close to the official values.
Two are off. The answer gives about 40 percent for internet use in Kenya, where the data show 35.0 percent in 2024, and 9 to 10 percent for growth in Rwanda in 2024, where the data show 7.2.
steps.speak: Two are off. The answer gives about forty percent for internet use in Kenya, where the data show thirty-five point zero percent in twenty twenty-four, and nine to ten percent for growth in Rwanda in twenty twenty-four, where the data show seven point two.

steps.say: No figure in the answer points to a record. A reader has no means to tell the close figures from the wrong ones.
An application builds the prompt from three parts. The builders write the instructions, the application selects the context, and the user writes the question.
Each part has its own slot, because a different person changes each one, at a different time.
The instructions become the system message. A model treats the system message as standing instructions for the whole exchange.
The context and the question go together into one user message, under fixed labels that let the model tell them apart.
These two messages hold everything the model reads in this call.
For the same question, the application now places four country briefs in the context. Each brief starts with its identifier in square brackets.
The grounded instructions tell the model to answer only from the context, to cite the identifier after each figure, and to say when something is missing.
The model compares the latest year, 2024, and writes an identifier after each figure.
steps.speak: The model compares the latest year, twenty twenty-four, and writes an identifier after each figure.

steps.say: Every figure now cites a brief. The 35.0 percent for internet use in Kenya comes from the Kenya digital brief.
steps.speak: Every figure now cites a brief. The thirty-five point zero percent for internet use in Kenya comes from the Kenya digital brief.

steps.say: A second question asks for the share of people in Kenya using the internet in 2025. The context holds only the Kenya digital brief, and its figures end in 2024.
steps.speak: A second question asks for the share of people in Kenya using the internet in twenty twenty-five. The context holds only the Kenya digital brief, and its figures end in twenty twenty-four.

steps.say: The model reports that the context has no figure for 2025. It names 2024 as the latest year and gives 35.0 percent with a citation.
steps.speak: The model reports that the context has no figure for twenty twenty-five. It names twenty twenty-four as the latest year and gives thirty-five point zero percent with a citation.

steps.say: This behaviour comes from one sentence of the grounded instructions.
The question “How connected is Kenya?” has several readings, among them internet use, mobile subscriptions, and broadband coverage.
Under basic instructions, the model chooses a reading itself. It answers at length on two readings and adds an analysis of growth beyond the question.
One added rule tells the model to list the readings and ask which one is meant. With that rule, the model asks before it answers.
A confident answer does not show the reader which reading the model chose. For a research application, one clarifying exchange removes that uncertainty.
A model reads a limited amount of text in each call. The limit is called the context window, and it is measured in tokens.
A token is a word or a part of a word, about four characters of English on average. The four briefs came to about a thousand tokens.
A collection of thousands of documents exceeds any context window. The price of a call also grows with the number of its tokens.
The application therefore selects, for each question, the passages that the model reads.
In the application, the answer shows the identifier of a brief after each figure.
A citation leads to the brief behind a figure. The Kenya digital brief states 35.0 percent for 2024, the latest year available.
steps.speak: A citation leads to the brief behind a figure. The Kenya digital brief states thirty-five point zero percent for twenty twenty-four, the latest year available.

steps.say: The Rwanda digital brief states 31.7 percent for the same year.
steps.speak: The Rwanda digital brief states thirty-one point seven percent for the same year.

steps.say: Instructions set the behaviour of the model. They make it cite each figure, report missing information, and ask about an ambiguous question.
Instructions cannot supply data. Each figure in a grounded answer comes from the evidence in the context.
Whether that evidence fits the question remains a judgement for the builders of the application and for the reader.
The citation makes that judgement easier, because a reader can open the cited brief and find the figure in its text.
